## Chapter 17

The leap into the unknown brought him first a fit of low spirits under the overpowering Maryland autumn—life too beautiful and too sad for one toned to November grays. Winter set him straight. He took modest bachelor rooms far out on G Street in a new house raised by a stranded Finn. Congress met. The old administration had weeks to run, but every eye strained toward the new. Office-seekers swarmed. Lost among them, he learned under cover, drifted unnoticed, and studied finance. He meant never to be a regular reporter; he lacked the ambition and pace; but he picked up friends on the press—reformers all—waiting with the rest for General Grant to give orders. Senators had nothing to say. One could only make notes.

Meanwhile Washington amused him. The place was a camp; there were no theatres, no restaurants, no monde, no demi-monde, no drives, no splendor, and, as Mme. de Struve said, no grandezza; yet for a young man it was paradise because they were few and in demand. After the abject unimportance of the young diplomat in London, he found himself a young duke in Washington, with ten stolen years of youth to make up and a ravenous appetite. The shabby town was lovable. Even the Washington girl—neither rich nor learned—had singular charm and used it. Three-fourths of existence proved social; politics and reform became the detail, and waltzing the profession. He wished he had reversed better in waltzing.

No one wanted knowledge. Washington was happier without style, and he in it—happier than ever before; happier than any one in a strenuous world could dream. But the life belonged to the eighteenth century and did not educate for the twentieth.

He worked, after a fashion; as much as the Government would have required for nine hundred dollars a year; and his work was not amusing. He gave three months to an article on the finances of the United States; Henry Reeve printed it, anonymous, in the Edinburgh Review. He wanted a place on that staff, under the vast shadow of Macaulay; thirty pounds a paper was pay and rank enough for vanity.

Then he stole for the North American a London device—an annual “Session”—and began a series meant to become political authority, supplementing the first paper with “Civil Service Reform.” Authentic history slipped in. Who read it he never knew. The fateful year 1870 was at hand, when quarterlies would give way to monthlies; letter-press to illustration; volumes to pages. He found himself fifty years behind his time, yet the drift still seemed conservative; the Church spoke with apparent authority; the quarterlies laid down an apparent law; truths a priori held their own against truths relative; according to Lowell, Right was forever on the scaffold, Wrong forever on the Throne; and a certain public still thought it believed it. He counted himself one more relic.

Meanwhile he, and four-fifths of the people, had united to elect Grant because the soldier represented order. A general who had commanded a million men could surely administer. “Let us have peace,” they echoed. He meant to support the Executive against the Senate, to take away its two-thirds vote and power of confirmation; safer in 1870 than in 1920. He even listened with relish to an exasperated Secretary’s maxim: “You can’t use tact with a Congressman! A Congressman is a hog! You must take a stick and hit him on the snout!” Innocently he asked: “If a Congressman is a hog, what is a Senator?” and saw executive officers petrify. The Senate’s egotism passed belief; faction had run so far under Andrew Johnson that hysteria became comic without ceasing to be mischievous.

With this temper he went to the Capitol to hear the Cabinet. Within five minutes he felt his future turned to absurdity. Grant’s nominations betrayed his incompetence as plainly as his intent: a great soldier might be a baby politician. Yet the list was not unfriendly. Hamilton Fish at State suggested conservative decency; George S. Boutwell at Treasury meant inertia—extinction for one like Henry Adams; Jacob D. Cox at Interior promised help; Judge Hoar, as Attorney-General, filled every ideal. One must still study Grant.

By chance Adam Badeau took rooms below him, and they dined together. Badeau—stout, red-faced, intelligent; an excellent military historian—talked much. Loyal to Grant and still more to Mrs. Grant, he held that no one except himself and Rawlins understood the General. Grant appeared an intermittent energy, immensely powerful when awake, passive and plastic in repose. Staff ideas were talked into him for weeks; in the end he announced them as his own and drove them with all his native force. They could never follow a process in his thought, nor be sure when he would act; they were not sure that he did think.

Badeau took him to the White House. He saw a dozen Presidents in his life; Grant most curious among them. A single word with him satisfied Henry that the fewer words he risked, the better. Only Garibaldi had given him the same impression: the intellect counted for nothing; only the energy counted. The type was pre-intellectual, archaic, and would have seemed so to cave-dwellers. Adam, according to legend, was such a man. One recognized the type elsewhere: forces of nature, energies of the prime, whose energies were the greater the less they wasted on thought; distrustful, shy, sometimes vindictive; dull in appearance; always needing stimulants, but for whom action was the highest stimulant—the instinct of fight. They made short work of scholars.

He did not feel Grant as hostile—only uncertain; superb and safe to follow in action; dangerous in torpor. Simple-minded, he resorted to commonplaces when at a loss: “Let us have peace!” “The best way to treat a bad law is to execute it.” Sometimes one doubted his good faith; he told a bright young woman in earnest that Venice would be a fine city if it were drained. In Mark Twain it would rank among his best witticisms; in Grant it measured simplicity. Lee betrayed the same commonplace in a Virginian form. What fretted Adams was his own education. Grant defied first principles. The idea that, as society grew older, it grew one-sided, upset evolution. That, two thousand years after Alexander and Caesar, a man like Grant should be called—and should truly be—the highest product of the most advanced evolution, made evolution ludicrous. The progress of evolution from President Washington to President Grant, was alone evidence enough to upset Darwin.

Yet the administration was not unfriendly; it was full of friends. Fish was almost kind; Cox sympathetic; Hoar ideal; but without the President and the Treasury, they could help little. Grant avowed a policy of drift; and a policy of drift attaches only barnacles. At thirty he had no notion of becoming a barnacle. His friends were reformers and critics; he himself an object of suspicion. Grant had no objects, wanted no help, wished for no champions. “Let us have peace!” meant: let me alone.

No one wanted to go into opposition. His hopes turned on finding an administration to support. He was for sale; he wanted to be bought; his price was cheap; he asked no office; he had his eye on New York; he only wanted something that would let itself be supported. Luck went dead against him. For once, he was fifty years in advance of his time.

## Chapter 18

The old New Englander lived solitary; the young sometimes human. Sam Hoar taught him the charm of Washington spring. The Potomac squandered beauty; Rock Creek was as wild as the Rockies; dogwood and judas-tree, azalea and laurel made the woods voluptuous; June thunder-gusts broke in terrific splendor. No European spring had shown him that intermixture of delicate grace and passionate depravity. He loved it too much and loitered into July, falling into the summer village ways about La Fayette Square as one whose rights of inheritance could not be questioned.

He found in himself a savage humor about Boston—the climate warring on society; sex a sort of crime; life as thin as the elms; but Boston’s thinness was in himself. He was trying to shape himself to his time; so was Boston; so was the country everywhere but Washington, where there were no surroundings to complain of.

Before he got back to Quincy, the effects of Grant’s character showed themselves. The attempt of Jay Gould to corner gold in September, 1869, has never been cleared up for him. Gould believed the Government would not interfere; he took precautions; he spent money to obtain assurances; yet he ventured. Any criminal lawyer must have begun by insisting that Gould had assurances from the White House or the Treasury, since none other would have satisfied him. To a young man idling at Quincy for want of a hire at three dollars a day, such scandal was Heaven-sent. He and his brother jumped at it; Charles took the railway history; Henry the gold story; they went to New York. He paid respects to the famous Jim Fisk in the Opera-House Palace, but the political mystery lay in Washington and he waited for Congress.

The Congressional investigation came. Material supplied by Government always lies under suspicion, but he soon knew all that was to be known. His friends—Fish, Cox, Hoar, Evarts, Sumner—were the most mystified. Their relations with White House and Treasury were not confidential; no one volunteered advice; press-men in private spoke with cynical frankness; the Committee dared not probe and refused to analyze. The trail faded whenever an Administration officer loomed. Every one dreaded to press inquiry. He himself feared to know too much. He had learned enough when he saw in evidence that Gould had stretched his net over the President’s closest surroundings, and that Boutwell’s incompetence lay at the bottom of Gould’s calculation. Publicly every one assured that the President had saved the situation; privately, that if not caught now he must be trapped next time, for the ways of Wall Street were dark and double.

That Grant should have fallen—or let Boutwell drop him—into such a morass within six months made the next four years—probably eight—possibly twelve—opaque to one who had hitched his wagon, as Emerson told him, to the star of reform. The worst scandals of the eighteenth century were harmless by the side of this, which smirched executive, judiciary, banks, corporate systems, professions, and people in one cesspool of vulgar corruption. By shutting one’s eyes, as though one were an Assistant Secretary, a writer might still help friends who were striving to give the Government an air of decency; but the Erie scandal was a mere incident. The same laxity that led Gould into a trap that might have become the penitentiary led the Senate, the Departments, and the Judiciary into cross-purposes that would have been scandalous in a girls’ boarding-school. Satirists prospered; audiences roared at caricatures of their own Senators. He laughed too, but for him the spectacle was no laughing matter. A young man has only one chance, and fools can extinguish it. One dull administration can drive out every active subordinate. In 1869–70 every intelligent man about Government prepared to go. The shrewdest was Mr. Boutwell, who turned out of the Treasury every one who could disturb his repose, and locked himself up in it alone. What he did there, no one knew. The Treasury ceased to exist as an active influence.

Warned that Boutwell meant to invite no support, he turned to State and Interior. He wanted no better; opposition was waste; an alliance with Northern Democrats and Southern rebels had never warmed to any Adams. Mr. Fish opened the Department freely; Sumner seemed inseparable from him; the policy safe. No mosquito could be so unlucky as to be caught again between Secretary and Senator.

The dream lasted hardly longer than in 1861. Sumner took possession of the Department; he seized the British mission for Motley; then unfolded a foreign policy of his own, to be forced on State and on Grant: he vetoed all tropical extension—St. Thomas and the Bay of Samaná went by; and, with incredulous stupor, one heard his plan to press every American claim against England with a view to compelling the cession of Canada. If war were the object, and Canada worth it, the scheme showed genius; if he thought England would cede Canada as a voluntary set-off to the Alabama Claims, he drivelled. Adams, lately from seven years in London, thought he knew as much about England as any one in Washington, and looked to Mr. Fish to say so. When at last Fish did say it, a year later, Sumner publicly cut his acquaintance.

The cross-purposes bewildered. There was a Department of State over which Fish nominally presided; a Department of Foreign Relations over which Sumner ruled at the Capitol; and a third Foreign Office in the War Department, with President Grant for chief, pressing West Indian extension. Grant’s simplicity was more disconcerting than Talleyrand’s complexity. Mr. Fish afterwards told him, grimly amused, that the President took a dislike to Motley because he parted his hair in the middle. Adams repeated it to Godkin, who made play with it till denial came. What of it? Men form judgments on less than hair. In truth Grant disliked Motley because they had nothing in common; for the same reason he disliked Sumner; and for the same he would be sure to dislike Adams, if given a chance.

A quarrel nearer home troubled him more. The Legal Tender decision, first stumbling-block to him in Washington, fell like a plaster ceiling and could not be escaped. He clung to the Supreme Court as a churchman to his bishops—his last rag of Right. Between Executive and Legislature, citizens have only Power; they had created the Court to protect against it. Frank Walker had promised the North American an article on the Legal Tender Act, founded on Spaulding’s account; Walker’s Census duties forced him to give Adams his notes; with the Chief Justice’s recollections, Adams completed the paper. He did not attack or defend Legal Tender; he meant to defend the Court and the Chief Justice. Walker’s army ferocity ran through it; Spaulding had cause to complain; historically the piece had value, demolishing the plea of necessity in 1862. The Chief Justice seemed pleased. Judge Hoar made no sign—then went on to demolish the Chief Justice. In spite of the best intentions, plainest self-interest, strongest wish to escape trouble, the article threw Adams into opposition. Hoar, like Boutwell, was implacable.

The Senate returned to irritated egotism. Scarcely a newspaper kept discipline; the New York Tribune was among the most criminal. Senators quarrelled with each other—and with the Executive—till every Department fell in confusion. They quarrelled with Hoar and drove him out. That Sumner and Hoar—two New Englanders in great place, most necessary to Henry’s success—should be the first victims of Grant’s lax rule must have had meaning for education, if he could have read it. He reflected for years. His four most powerful friends had matched themselves two and two, fighting to a finish—Sumner–Fish; Chase–Hoar—with foreign affairs and the judiciary for prizes. What was the value, in education, of such a fight?

The newspapers harped on jobs and moral laxity. Society hesitated, pitilessly sacrificing the weak, deferentially following the strong. In spite of criticism, the public nominated Grant, Garfield, and Blaine, and voted for them. Young men were forced to see that either a new standard must be created, or none upheld. The moral law had expired—like the Constitution.

He crammed his “Session” of 1869–70 with what he had seen and been told. It proved his last study in current politics and his dying testament as a humble member of the press. The system of 1789 had broken down, and with it the eighteenth‑century fabric of a priori, or moral, principles. Grant’s administration marked the avowal. Nine‑tenths of men’s political energies must henceforth be wasted on expedients to piece out—to patch—or, in vulgar language, to tinker—the political machine as often as it broke down. Such a system, or want of system, might last centuries, tempered by an occasional revolution or civil war; but, as a machine, it was, or soon would be, the poorest in the world—the clumsiest—the most inefficient.

If this were education, its worth was doubtful. Looking up to its loftiest results—Mr. Boutwell, Mr. Conkling, even Mr. Sumner—one could not say the schooling, when it carried one to those heights, was worth anything. Clever, amusing men on lower levels made fun of the demi‑gods and used of Grant a language no review would print. What was to become of them in turn? What political ambition would such education breed? Society wanted a system that worked and men who could work it; it found neither. He had tried his hands and failed. He was driven, with thousands of young men, into active enmity, not only to Grant, but to the system that took possession of him. Every hope that had brought him to Washington proved absurd. No one wanted him; no one wanted reformers; the blackmailer alone was the normal product of politics as of business.

All this was excessively amusing. He had never been so busy, so interested, so in the thick. He knew Congressmen by scores, newspaper-men by the dozen; wrote attacks and defences for his organs; was as happy as professional brokers of influence; happier than Fish, J. D. Cox, Chief Justice Chase, Attorney-General Hoar, or Charles Sumner. When spring came he took to the woods, which were best of all. After the first of April, “the vast maternity” of nature showed charms more voluptuous than the vast paternity of the Senate. Senators were less ornamental than dogwood or the judas-tree; less good company. A distant glimpse of the dome, over miles of foliage, lent the Capitol a purified charm. One thought of St. Peter’s and the steps of Ara Cœli.

He shortened his spring. He needed London. He had finished his “Gold Conspiracy,” the best work he had done; he meant it for Reeve and the Edinburgh, to strike Erie where it was exposed—socially and financially. Anything about America in an English review was reprinted in America entire. He wanted to be pirated and advertised free of charge; pay in any case was nothing. Under the excitement of chase, he was becoming a pirate himself, and liked it.
